list.listitem: Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome refers to the triad of short PR interval, delta waves on the ECG (pre-excitation), and tachyarrhythmias. C
Atrioventricular re-entry tachycardia represents 95% of re-entrant tachycardias occurring in patients with WPW syndrome. B
There is a small risk of sudden cardiac death secondary to rapid conduction of atrial fibrillation to the ventricles, degenerating into ventricular fibrillation. B

Long-term medical therapy that is an option in patients with WPW and includes drugs like propafenone, flecainide, sotalol, and amiodarone. Monotherapy with Digoxin, verapamil, diltiazem, and beta blockers should be avoided. B
For symptomatic and high-risk patients, catheter ablation is recommended. A

background.definition: The term Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome is reserved for patients with both electrocardiographic pre-excitation and symptomatic tachyarrhythmias. Electrocardiographic pre-excitation refers to the presence of a delta wave (slurring of the initial part of the QRS, resulting in widening) and a short PR interval.

list.listitem: Delta waves detectable on an ECG are present in 0.15% to 0.25% of the general population.
The incidence of sudden cardiac death is 0.47% to 0.60% per year.
One-third of patients with WPW also have atrial fibrillation.
Congenital
Rare familial variety
Also known to be associated with congenital heart disease, such as Ebstein’s anomaly
Accessory pathways represent the remnants of failed fusion of AV junctional tissue.

Multiple accessory pathways may be seen, especially in children and in patients with Ebstein’s anomaly. Such pathways often exhibit faster conduction than is seen in normal conduction tissue such as the AV node.

Accessory pathways can have conduction in either antegrade or retrograde directions or both. Electrophysiologic properties differ from patient to patient and depend on age, autonomic tone, and location.
This “bypass” of the normal AV node by the accessory pathway allows depolarization of the ventricular muscle earlier than would occur otherwise, resulting in the delta wave.
Patients most often present with palpitations associated with dizziness or syncope, or have preexcitation diagnosed by ECGs obtained for other reasons. C
The term WPW is restricted to the triad of short PR interval, widened QRS secondary to the delta wave, and tachyarrhythmias. A
Symptomatic and high-risk patients require electrophysiologic studies for both risk stratification and curative ablation.
Arrhythmias that are accessory pathway mediated can be narrow (Orthodromic AVRT) or wide (antidromic AVRT) depending on the retrograde or anterograde use of the accessory pathway.
Nonreentrant arrythmias such as atrial tachycardia,fibrillation may use the accessory pathway as a bystander to activate the ventricles.
Rapid wide complex irregularly irregular rhythm with bizarre QRS morphology should suggest pre-excited atrial fibrillation, a potentially lethal rhythm.

Differential.Differential_Features: Absence of delta wave, short RP tachycardia, pseudo R prime may be seen in V1, or pseudo S waves in inferior. May need diagnostic electrophysiologic study
Absence of delta waves; extremely rapid rates with delta waves suggest WPW
Absence of delta wave and diagnostic findings on electrophysiologic studies
Difficult to differentiate from atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardias on ECG; electrophysiologic studies are needed

list.listitem: Most patients present in the first 4 decades of life with episodes of palpitations that may be associated with symptoms of cerebral hypoperfusion, such as dizziness and/or syncope due to high ventricular rates.
Additional arrhythmia-related symptoms include chest discomfort and dyspnea.
Patients noted to have characteristic features on ECGs obtained for other reasons constitute another common presentation.
If WPW is clinically suspected, the initial test is resting ECG. This can demonstrate the characteristic short PR interval and presence of delta waves.
Tachyarrhythmias associated with accessory pathways are most commonly atrioventricular reentrant tachycardias.

Atrial fibrillation with rapid conduction to the ventricles via accessory pathways with short antegrade refractory periods is another important arrhythmia. Rapid ventricular rates can occasionally degenerate to ventricular fibrillation.

The clinician should be aware that delta waves on occasion may be subtle or, in cases of “concealed” accessory pathways, be absent. The degree of pre-excitation on the surface ECG depends on the conduction properties of both the AV node and the accessory pathway. Certain algorithms such as the Arruda algorithm use the polarity of the delta wave on surface ECG to help predict the approximate anatomic location.
Certain findings such as intermittent, exercise-induced, or drug-induced loss of pre-excitation can identify low risk if the patient is asymptomatic.
Electrophysiologic studies are used to locate accessory pathways which then can be ablated using radiofrequency catheter ablation.

Order a resting ECG if arrhythmia is clinically suspected (palpitations, syncope, dizziness, chest pain). If pre-excitation is noted on ECG that suggests WPW, consider referral to an electrophysiologist.
If patient shows no pre-excitation and has no history of syncope, consider ordering an event monitor.

Intravenous beta blockers, digoxin, adenosine, and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers slow AV nodal conduction; they are contraindicated in patients with WPW with pre-excited tachycardia as they can accelerate the ventricular rate and produce ventricular fibrillation. B
In patients who develop symptomatic tachycardia in whom invasive strategy is not applicable, long-term medical therapy includes propafenone, flecainide, sotalol, and amiodarone. B
Catheter ablation is recommended for patients with poorly tolerated WPW syndrome. A
Treatment is not recommended for asymptomatic patients, B but electrophysiological study can be considered in certain special situations. C

In hemodynamically stable patients with WPW, IV amiodarone or procainamide may be used. For hemodynamically unstable presentations, electrical cardioversion and advanced cardiac life support protocols are indicated.

Intravenous beta blockers, digoxin, adenosine, lidocaine, and nondihydropyridine-calcium channel blockers slow AV nodal conduction and are contraindicated in patients with WPW with tachycardia associated with ventricular pre-excitation. They can increase conduction along the accessory pathway resulting in acceleration of the ventricular rate, which produces ventricular fibrillation.

In patients who develop atrioventricular reentrant tachycardias, atrial fibrillation, or flutter in whom radiofrequency ablation is not considered, propafenone, flecainide, sotalol, or amiodarone may be used to control arrhythmias. Pure AV-nodal blockers such as adenosine, beta blockers, verapamil, diltiazem, and digoxin as chronic monotherapy are avoided in patients with WPW syndrome.
Catheter-based radiofrequency ablation is performed in conjunction with an electrophysiology study. The initial success rate is usually greater than 95% in most series.

Indications for ablation in asymptomatic patients: The positive predictive value of routine electrophysiologic testing is too low to justify testing. ACC/ESC guidelines restrict ablation to certain professions and on individual consideration.The relatively low incidence of sudden cardiac death and low risk of supraventricular tachycardia in subjects with WPW type pre-excitation support this recommendation.
Risk stratification can help identify candidacy for ablation.

Symptomatic patients: Catheter ablation is recommended in patients with WPW syndrome with frequent symptoms. It is also an option for patients with single or infrequent atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia episodes.
The overall complication rate is between 1% and 4% and incidence of death from the procedure is 0.2%. Recurrences of arrhythmias occur in 3% to 5% of successful catheter ablation procedures.
One-third of asymptomatic patients with pre-excited ECGs eventually develop symptoms; it is uncommon for new symptoms to develop in a patient who has been asymptomatic until age 40 years. B

In symptomatic patients seen in tertiary referral centers the prevalence of aborted sudden cardiac death is 2% to 11%. Population-based studies indicate that sudden cardiac death is a very rare (0.15% per year) presentation in patients with WPW syndrome. B
